newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Arthuis sees euro as major reserve currency.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Arthuis sees euro as major reserve currency.

text.p: French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said on Thursday he saw the euro quickly becoming a major reserve currency which would allow trade to be based on currency parities which better reflected economic fundamentals.

"As regards our trade with other countries, the euro, which is destined to become quickly a major world reserve currency, will allow it to be founded on parities which better reflect the real economic fundamentals of each country," he said.

France is keen to use the launch of Europe's single currency on January 1, 1999 to give the bloc the power to fight against any devaluation in the dollar which would give U.S. exporters an unfair advantage over their European rivals.
The dollar is currently the world's leading reserve currency -- the preferred holding of central banks and unit of account in international trade -- followed by the mark.

French officials say the importance of the dollar in world trade allowed the United States to let the dollar fall without paying the price of devaluation in terms of higher interest rates and want Europe to be able to do the same with the euro.
Its call to use the euro as what could effectively be a trade weapon has raised hackles among some who fear it would undermine the fledgling currency from the start.

Its demand for an economic council to coordinate economic and exchange rate policy inside the euro zone has also raised fears it might try to use this to influence the monetary policy of the future independent European Central Bank.
Arthuis on Thursday repeated a call for such a stability council, which French officials see as Europe's equivalent of the informal Group of Seven (G7) rich nations forum.

"I will develop the idea of a stability and growth council, an informal occasion responsible for allowing the countries using the euro to coordinate their economic policies better," he told a conference at export credit guarantee agency COFACE.
Former Bundesbank President Karl Otto Poehl said earlier this week that he found the French proposals very worrying.

Poehl, who resigned from the Bundesbank in 1991, said the reason for launching the euro was never meant to be to create a new reserve currency, nor to fight the caprices of financial markets, as French officials have suggested.

"In my understanding this is not the reason for the creation of monetary union to create a counterweight to the dollar. It is not the reason to forge the euro into a second reserve currency," he said, adding its role as a reserve currency could be an end-product rather than a cause.
"In Germany the creation of an economic and monetary union is the elimination of foreign exchange risk...the creation of a genuine internal market," he said.
